canonical_topic: Geographic drivers of solar production and capacity factor
definition: Solar output depends on installation type and location, with proximity to the equator and dry/arid climate both increasing production, and capacity factor measuring realized AC output against a unit's rated size.
core_idea: Solar farms closer to the equator in dry climates produce more power because sunlight travels through less atmosphere and loses less energy, and this locational effect is one driver behind a unit's capacity factor.
key_points: Dry, arid climates near the equator yield the highest solar production.
Greater distance from the equator means sunlight passes through more atmosphere, reducing the energy content that reaches the panel and lowering production.
Example comparison: a Desert Southwest (e.g., Arizona) solar farm would produce more power than one in the northeastern U.S. (e.g., New Jersey).
Capacity factor is the ratio of actual power delivered to the grid versus the unit's stated (rated) size.
Example given: a 100-KW installation delivering 70 KW of AC power has a 70 percent capacity factor.
A ~70 percent capacity factor is described as typical when a unit's size is stated relative to its DC output at midday.
relationships: Connects to DC-to-AC conversion losses, since capacity factor as defined here is measured in AC terms against a DC-based rating.
trading_implications: Location selection (latitude, aridity) is a first-order driver of expected capacity factor and thus expected generation revenue.
caveats: A stated capacity factor of ~70% for solar is tied to comparing AC output against a midday DC rating, not an inherent universal solar constant.

formulas.name: Capacity factor
formulas.formula: Capacity Factor = AC Power Delivered to Grid / Rated Unit Size

variables.AC Power Delivered to Grid: actual power output placed onto the grid, kW or MW
variables.Rated Unit Size: stated nameplate size of the installation, typically DC kW/MW at midday
